The family line of Jesus

From Adam to Jesus, as traced in Matthew 1 and Luke 3. Tap anyone to learn who they were and find every mention of them.

Both Gospels Matthew only Luke only
Why are there two different lists? +

Matthew starts with Abraham and moves forward, arranging the names in three sets of fourteen. To keep that pattern he leaves out some kings, such as Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, and Jehoiakim. Luke starts with Jesus and works backward past Abraham to Adam, “the son of God.”

The two lists agree from Abraham to David. Then Matthew follows King Solomon while Luke follows Nathan, another son of David and Bathsheba (1 Chronicles 3:5). They meet briefly at Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, then part again until Joseph.

How churches explain the difference

Both lists are Joseph's. An early explanation from Julius Africanus (around AD 220), long held in Catholic and Orthodox tradition: Joseph's father by birth and his legal father were linked through a levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), so one list is natural and the other legal.

Luke gives Mary's line. Many Protestants read Heli as Mary's father, with Joseph called his “son” by marriage. That would make Luke's list Jesus' physical ancestry, since both Gospels teach he was born of a virgin.

Royal line and human line. Many readers see Matthew showing Jesus' legal right to David's throne through the kings, and Luke showing his tie to all humanity back to Adam.

Details readers notice

Matthew names five women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba (“the wife of Urias”), and Mary. Luke includes a second Cainan, found in the Greek Septuagint but not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11. Jeremiah 22:30 says no descendant of Jeconiah would rule from David's throne; some see the virgin birth as the answer to that.

Angels and demons

The ranks, names, and titles found in Scripture and Christian tradition. Tap any rank or name for details; every verse cited is listed at the bottom.

The heavenly host

The Bible names these orders but never ranks them. This nine-level arrangement comes from The Celestial Hierarchy by Pseudo-Dionysius (around AD 500), later taught by Thomas Aquinas and pictured by Dante.

Closest to God

The powers of darkness

Satan heads the fallen angels. Ephesians 6:12 lists four kinds of evil powers; whether Paul meant them as a ranking is debated.

How churches differ

Catholic and Orthodox teaching commonly uses the nine choirs and affirms guardian angels (Matthew 18:10). Both honor Raphael, named in Tobit. Orthodox tradition also venerates seven archangels, including Uriel, Selaphiel, Jegudiel, and Barachiel.

Most Protestants affirm that angels and demons are real but treat the nine-level ranking as speculation. Only Michael and Gabriel are named in their 66-book Bible.

Seventh-day Adventists teach that Michael the archangel is Christ himself, and that Lucifer, once a covering cherub, began the great controversy between good and evil.

Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Michael is Jesus in his heavenly existence, and that Satan was cast out of heaven in 1914.

Latter-day Saints teach that Michael was Adam before mortal life, identify Gabriel with Noah, and teach that Lucifer rebelled in a premortal council.

On Lucifer: Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 have long been read as describing Satan's fall. Many scholars, and some churches, read them first as taunts against the kings of Babylon and Tyre, with any reference to Satan as secondary.

    Saints

    Search by name to read about a saint's life, feast day, and when they were canonized.

    When they were made saints

    Canonized by a popeGlorified by an Orthodox church

    How churches recognize saints

    Before canonization existed. For the first thousand years, saints were recognized by local acclaim, usually martyrs and bishops whose churches kept the day of their death. That's why the apostles and early saints here were never formally canonized. The first known papal canonization was Ulrich of Augsburg in 993, and popes took sole control of the process in 1234.

    Catholic. A cause moves through four stages: Servant of God, Venerable (a life of heroic virtue), Blessed (beatification, usually after one approved miracle), and Saint (canonization, usually after a second). Martyrs can be beatified without a miracle. The pope declares a canonization, and Catholics may ask saints to pray for them.

    Orthodox. Saints are “glorified” rather than canonized, by the synod of a self-governing church, usually after widespread local veneration. Orthodox churches honor many saints from before 1054 that Catholics share, and some churches keep feasts on the older Julian calendar, 13 days later.

    Anglican and Lutheran. These churches keep calendars of saints and commemorations, including figures like Martin Luther, Thomas Cranmer, and Dietrich Bonhoeffer, but they don't canonize. They honor saints as examples of faith rather than asking for their prayers.

    Most other Protestants. The New Testament calls all believers “saints” (Romans 1:7, Ephesians 1:1). Baptists, Pentecostals, and non-denominational churches generally don't keep saints' days and pray only to God.

    Latter-day Saints and Jehovah's Witnesses. Latter-day Saints use “saints” for all church members, as in the church's name. Neither group venerates saints.

    Feast days follow the Catholic calendar unless noted; some are observed only in certain countries. Canonizations are current through October 2025.

    How the Bible's books were decided

    Tap a dot to read about each step.

    Which Bibles include it: P In the Bible P In an appendix P Not included E Not confirmed P = Protestant, C = Catholic, O = Eastern Orthodox, E = Ethiopian Orthodox

    How churches decided what belongs

    No single meeting picked the Bible's books. Churches recognized them over centuries, mostly by asking four questions: Is it apostolic, written by an apostle or someone close to one? Is it orthodox, agreeing with the faith the churches already held? Is it catholic, used widely across the churches rather than in one region? And is it ancient, dating from the time of the apostles or the prophets?

    The New Testament is the same 27 books in Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Bibles. Most were accepted early; Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, and Revelation were debated longer. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts 81 books in all, the most of any church, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees; see the Ethiopian Bible section above.

    The Old Testament is where churches differ. Protestants follow the Hebrew Bible used by Jews, 39 books. Catholics add 7 books plus parts of Esther and Daniel, for 46. Orthodox churches add a few more, following the Greek Old Testament the early Church used.

    Latter-day Saints use the KJV without the Apocrypha. Their scripture says of the Apocrypha, “There are many things contained therein that are true,” along with additions by men, and that reading it is helpful but not needed (Doctrine and Covenants 91). Jehovah's Witnesses use the 66 books.

    Dates are scholarly estimates and many are debated. Reading links go to public-domain texts at eBible.org and the Internet Archive, which open in a new tab; a few older archive scans are large files. Translations from 1913 and earlier use older English.
